Roneat Ek is the xylophone used in Cambodian classical music, its sounding classification idiophone; it is also called Roneat Rut. The body is a curved, elongated boat shape, made of a wooden soundbox with 21 bamboo or hardwood bars; the bars are suspended by cords from the two end walls so that they do not touch the frame, and they are tuned with lumps of a wax and lead mixture. The player strikes with two wooden mallets, and in the pinpeat (Pinpeat) and mahori (Mahori) orchestras it leads, gives the opening and cues the other instruments, and in that ensemble it stands to the right of the lower xylophone, Roneat Thung.
Roneat Ek 為體鳴樂器，以兩根木槌敲擊21根竹或硬木音條發聲；音條以繩懸: Roneat Ek is an idiophone, sounded by striking 21 bamboo or hardwood bars with two wooden mallets; the bars are suspended by cords from the two walls of the soundbox without touching the edges, and the mallet heads are wrapped in cloth and hold lumps of wax and lead for tuning, so that the pitches can be tuned into the Cambodian scale. The source does not say how volume is controlled. Its range runs from the highest bar at the right end, 25 centimetres, to the lowest at the left, 40 centimetres, without absolute note names. Compared with the related Roneat Thung it is higher in range, and in the pinpeat (Pinpeat) and mahori (Mahori) ensembles it takes the lead, gives the opening and cues the other instruments; the other name roneat rut (meaning the running xylophone) points to the effect of continuous running across the bars.

柬埔寨木琴主要用於柬埔寨古典音樂，在皮帕特合奏中演奏，通常位於音域較低的同族木琴: The Cambodian xylophone is used mainly in Cambodian classical music, played in the pinpeat ensemble, where it usually stands to the right of the related xylophone of lower range. The etymology notes also say that it takes part in the mahori ensemble and has a leading role, able to open a piece and cue the other instruments. The source mentions no particular composer or work, so listening examples are best understood through these two kinds of traditional ensemble.
柬埔寨木琴的起源可追溯至扶南時期，音樂與舞蹈已在寺廟中演出；因同類低音樂器在吳哥: The origin of the Cambodian xylophone can be traced to the Funan period, when music and dance were already performed in the temples; because a related lower instrument had entered the ensemble before Angkor, researchers think it is earlier than Angkor. Stone xylophones in the central highlands of Vietnam and in central Cambodia point to an older tradition. New techniques have identified images of ensembles that include a xylophone on the walls of Angkor Wat, perhaps the earliest depiction. Another source says it was influenced by Javanese gamelan and spread north-west to Burma; in 802 Jayavarman II returned from Java and established the rite of the god-king. Later it is often seen in wall paintings and in the pinpeat and mohori ensembles.
琴身（音箱）以優質木材製成，來源列 neang nuon、beng等木名。發聲體: The body (soundbox) is made of good-quality wood, the source giving the wood names neang nuon and beng. The sounding body is twenty-one bamboo or hardwood bars, the source also giving krannoong, beng and neang nuon; the bars are threaded and suspended on nylon cord. At both ends underneath, the bars carry promor (a mixture of wax and lead) for tuning. The mallets are of the same wood as the body, with promor heads wrapped in two or three layers of cloth and bound with thread. The other materials are not stated.
站於琴前，雙手持棒敲擊琴鍵中央。手持樂器本體，透過敲擊、搖晃、刮奏或撥彈等方式使: Stand in front of the instrument and strike the middle of the keys with a stick in each hand. You hold the instrument itself and make it vibrate by striking, shaking, scraping or plucking. Different parts and different amounts of force give different timbres. In practice, first confirm the correct way of holding the instrument, and once the basic way of sounding it is in hand, go on to rhythms and melodies. Fingers or drumsticks strike the surface and the bounce brings them back naturally, with the wrist relaxed.
